question: What is the primary purpose of the controlling function in nursing management?

options.A: To punish staff members who make clinical errors
options.B: To monitor performance against standards and take corrective action
options.C: To create the initial strategic plan for the hospital
options.D: To recruit new nursing personnel for the unit

explanation: Controlling involves monitoring performance, comparing it to established goals, and making corrections to ensure standards are met. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h1)

question: Why is effective control especially important in Nigerian healthcare settings?

options.A: It guarantees unlimited funding from international donors
options.B: It helps manage scarce resources and ensures safe, efficient care
options.C: It eliminates the need for any nursing documentation
options.D: It prevents patients from ever experiencing complications

explanation: Because resources can be scarce and workloads heavy, control mechanisms ensure optimal resource utilization and high standards of care. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h1)

question: What is the very first step in the controlling process?
explanation: The controlling process always begins with establishing the standards and benchmarks against which future performance will be measured. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h2)

question: During which step of the controlling process does a nurse manager identify variances?
explanation: Variances are identified when the manager compares actual clinical performance data against the pre-established standards. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h2)

question: Which type of control is implemented before an activity begins to prevent problems?
explanation: Feedforward controls are proactive measures implemented before care delivery to prevent issues before they occur. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h3)

question: Routine ward rounds and real-time supervision of medication administration are examples of which type of control?
explanation: Concurrent controls take place while the care or activity is actively happening, allowing for immediate correction of mistakes. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h3)

question: An indicator that measures the rate of hospital-acquired pressure injuries in a ward is an example of which type of standard?
explanation: Outcome standards and indicators measure the end result of care provided, such as complication rates or patient recovery status. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h4)

question: What does the acronym SMART stand for in the context of setting performance standards?
explanation: SMART is a widely accepted framework for setting clear goals, standing for Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of conducting regular nursing chart audits?

options.A: To punish nurses who have poor handwriting
options.B: To check if care plans and vital signs are documented correctly
options.C: To calculate the hospital's annual profit margin
options.D: To determine which patients should be discharged immediately

explanation: Chart audits allow managers to review documentation practices and ensure that clinical care tasks are properly recorded. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h5)

question: Why is it important for performance measurement tools to be objective and perceived as fair by nursing staff?

options.A: To eliminate the need for any nursing leadership
options.B: To prevent defensiveness and data falsification among staff
options.C: To ensure patients pay their hospital bills on time
options.D: To reduce the number of nursing shifts per week

explanation: When data tools are seen as fair and objective, staff are less likely to hide errors or falsify records, leading to more accurate quality data. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h5)

question: What should a nurse manager do first when a performance deviation is identified?

options.B: Evaluate and investigate the root cause of the deviation
options.C: Ignore the deviation if no patient died
options.D: Rewrite all hospital policies and standards

explanation: Understanding the root cause is essential before taking corrective action, ensuring fixes address systemic issues rather than just symptoms. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h6)

question: What is the benefit of fostering a 'just culture' when addressing clinical errors and deviations?

options.A: It ensures staff feel safe reporting mistakes so system fixes can be made
options.B: It eliminates all responsibility and accountability for individual nurses
options.C: It stops patients from ever filing formal complaints
options.D: It reduces the hospital's expenditure on medical supplies

explanation: A just culture encourages open reporting of near-misses and errors, allowing managers to fix underlying systemic problems without inducing fear. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h6)

question: Which of the following is a primary example of a patient safety control in nursing practice?

options.B: Executing surgical safety checklists and hand hygiene audits

explanation: Surgical safety checklists and hand hygiene audits are direct, practical controls used to safeguard patients from avoidable harm. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h7)

question: What is the main purpose of quality assurance (QA) programs in healthcare organizations?

options.A: To increase the workload of staff nurses
options.B: To systematically monitor operations and ensure standards of quality are met
options.D: To reduce the number of registered nurses on duty

explanation: QA programs involve systematic monitoring to ensure that clinical services consistently meet established quality standards. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h7)

question: What is a common reason why nursing staff might resist control systems in a healthcare facility?

options.A: They believe the controls are too easy to pass
options.B: They perceive them as punitive tools rather than supportive measures
options.C: They have too much free time on their shifts
options.D: They prefer working without any clinical guidelines

explanation: Resistance often occurs when staff view controls as punitive monitoring devices rather than supportive frameworks for professional practice. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h8)

question: Which strategy helps a nurse manager successfully overcome resistance to control systems?

options.A: Implementing all new rules in secret without informing the staff
options.B: Involving nurses in designing the control systems and providing transparent feedback
options.C: Increasing disciplinary punishments for minor paperwork errors
options.D: Eliminating all audits and performance reviews completely

explanation: Involving staff in the design process and maintaining transparency builds trust and encourages cooperation with control mechanisms. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h8)
